title: Push/fold
summary: With 10 BB or less: why all-in or fold beats a normal open, and how wide to push and call.

why.text: At 10–12 BB a normal open breaks the stack: you put in 2.2 BB, face a 3-bet all-in, and calling with a weak hand is bad while folding gives up a fifth of your stack. Going **all-in right away** wins two ways: the opponent folds (**fold equity**) or you win the showdown.

ev.text: EV of a push = **fold chance × pot** + **call chance × result of the all-in**. Example: small blind, 10 BB, the pot holds 1.5 BB. If the big blind folds 60% of the time, the folds alone bring 0.6 × 1.5 = 0.9 BB, and in the other 40% you still have equity against its calling range.

push.caption: Small blind against the big blind, 10 BB: a simplified push range (about half of all hands).

call.caption: Big blind against a 10 BB push: a simplified calling range (about a third of all hands).

asym.text:
Why pushes are wider than calls: the pusher has fold equity, the caller has none. To call an all-in you need a hand that beats the pushing range on its own. So the calling range is always narrower than the pushing range.

The shorter the stack, the wider the push: with 5 BB the small blind pushes almost everything.

q-a7.q: You have 8 BB on the button, everyone folded to you. What is usually best with A7o?
options: Open 2 BB and fold to a 3-bet
q-a7.explain: At 8 BB an ace is a clear push: fold equity plus decent equity when called.

t1.q: Why are pushes wider than calls?
t1.explain: Folds make a push profitable even with a weaker hand; a call wins only at showdown.

t2.q: How does the push range change as the stack gets shorter?
t2.explain: The blinds become a bigger share of the stack, and waiting costs more.

t3.q: What makes up the EV of a push?
options: The opponent’s folds and the all-in result when he calls
t3.explain: Both parts count; that is why weak hands can push and must not call.
